name: Double eyelid surgery (Asian blepharoplasty)

lead: Double eyelid surgery forms a crease in the upper eyelid for people whose lids lack one. The payoff is a defined lid line and eyes that look larger and more open.

It is among the most popular cosmetic procedures in many East Asian countries, particularly South Korea, with operations typically lasting 30 to 60 minutes. The literature is large but mostly surgical case series, including patient-reported outcome studies such as a FACE-Q validation of 200 cases.

paras: Surgeons use incisional approaches, which fix the skin to deeper lid structures through a cut, and suture approaches that use buried stitches. It is often combined with epicanthoplasty. Stitches are typically removed after 5 to 7 days, and the crease settles as swelling goes down.
The literature describes static or overly depressed folds, multiple folds, asymmetry and failed folds that need revision, plus suture-related problems with buried-suture methods.

angle.text: Double eyelid surgery forms an upper-lid crease, giving more lid definition and a larger, more open-looking eye. The result is visible after healing. It is among the most commonly performed cosmetic procedures in East Asia, studied mostly in surgical case series.

lead: Double eyelid surgery, also called Asian blepharoplasty or supratarsal fold creation, is an operation that forms a crease in the upper eyelid. Surgical authors note that Asian upper lids often have no superior palpebral fold, along with excess fat, pretarsal skin laxity and a medial epicanthal fold.[1]

Wikipedia describes it as among the most popular cosmetic procedures in many East Asian countries, particularly South Korea, with typical operations lasting 30 to 60 minutes and sutures removed after 5 to 7 days.[2] Authors in the plastic surgery literature say preferences for double eyelids have grown with cultural exchange.[1]

Methods fall broadly into incisional and suture (non-incisional) approaches. Evidence is mostly retrospective surgical series; a FACE-Q validation study measured patient satisfaction in 200 cases.[3][4][5]

paras: Authors describe the characteristic features of the Asian upper eyelid as lack of a superior palpebral fold, abundant fat, pretarsal skin laxity and a medial epicanthal fold, and report that many Asians regard double eyelids as attractive.[1] A review describes the anatomy of the Asian upper eyelid, patient assessment, an external incisional technique and pitfalls.[4]

Wikipedia distinguishes double eyelid surgery in younger patients, aimed at creating a fold, from Asian blepharoplasty in older patients, which can also remove surplus skin. It notes that the term blepharoplasty dates to 1818.[2]

The incisional method uses an upper lid incision with deeper fixation. Variants include orbicularis oculi to levator aponeurosis fixation,[6] and a technique using septoaponeurosis junctional thickening, reported in 680 patients, designed to produce a dynamic fold and avoid a static overdepressed one.[3] Buried-suture methods avoid a skin incision and are covered in the article on non-incisional double eyelid surgery.
Epicanthoplasty is often added; techniques including Y-V advancement and 'lazy S-curve' epicanthoplasty have been described.[1][7][8]

Reported problems include static folds,[3] multiple upper-lid folds requiring correction,[9] and failed folds requiring corrective revision, discussed in a 2004 paper on strategies after previously failed revisions.[10]
A retrospective study validated FACE-Q appearance satisfaction scales for minor-incision double-eyelid blepharoplasty in 200 young Asian patients.[5]

Wikipedia reports that many foreigners travel to South Korea for the procedure and cites cost estimates of roughly US$2,000 to $4,000, depending on technique and surgeon. Its references include scholarship on the 'Korean Look' and medical nationalism, indicating the topic is also studied as a cultural phenomenon.[2]

Human evidence is dominated by surgical case series and technique reports,[3][1][4][7][10][8][9] plus a FACE-Q validation study.[5] A registered, unrandomised study (NCT04001660, 30 participants) examined subbrow blepharoplasty combined with double eyelid surgery in Asian women.[11] No large randomised comparison of techniques was found.

timeline.event: The term 'blepharoplasty' is coined by von Graefe (per Wikipedia).[2]
Strategies for corrective surgery after failed Asian blepharoplasty published.[10]
Septoaponeurosis junctional thickening technique reported in 680 patients.[3]
FACE-Q scales validated for double-eyelid blepharoplasty in young Asians.[5]
